title: The Carmichael Function on Odd Prime Powers: λ(pᵏ) = pᵏ⁻¹(p − 1)
description: Sibling of euler-totient-oq-01-oq-02 (verified). The parent records only the coincidence λ(pᵏ) = φ(pᵏ) for odd primes, leaving λ implicit. This entry supplies the explicit closed form λ(pᵏ) = pᵏ⁻¹(p − 1) and the structural reason it holds: (ℤ/pᵏℤ)ˣ is cyclic, so its exponent (which is λ) equals its order (which is φ). Every link of the chain cyclic ⟹ exponent = order ⟹ λ(pᵏ) = φ(pᵏ) = pᵏ⁻¹(p − 1) is made explicit, a primitive root (a unit of order exactly φ(pᵏ)) is exhibited, and concrete values λ(9)=6, λ(27)=18, λ(25)=20, λ(7)=6, λ(49)=42 are derived. 0 axioms, 0 sorries.

overview.historicalContext: The Carmichael function λ(n) is the reduced totient — the exponent of the unit group (ℤ/nℤ)ˣ — and always divides Euler's totient φ(n), the group's order, with equality exactly when the group is cyclic. The two prime-power regimes are opposite. For powers of two with k ≥ 3 the group (ℤ/2ᵏℤ)ˣ ≅ ℤ/2 × ℤ/2ᵏ⁻² is non-cyclic and λ(2ᵏ) = 2ᵏ⁻² = φ(2ᵏ)/2 (the parent entry's headline). For an odd prime p the group (ℤ/pᵏℤ)ˣ is cyclic — Gauss's primitive-root theorem — so λ(pᵏ) = φ(pᵏ), and the totient prime-power formula φ(pᵏ) = pᵏ⁻¹(p − 1) turns this into a closed polynomial in p and k. The existence of a primitive root mod pᵏ (an element whose powers exhaust all units) is the classical companion fact, governing the period of base-p reciprocals and the structure of every cyclic discrete logarithm.
overview.problemStatement: For an odd prime p and k ≥ 1, prove λ(pᵏ) = pᵏ⁻¹(p − 1), exhibiting the mechanism: (ℤ/pᵏℤ)ˣ is cyclic, hence its exponent equals its order, hence λ(pᵏ) = φ(pᵏ) = pᵏ⁻¹(p − 1). Establish the k = 1 case λ(p) = p − 1, the existence of a primitive root (a unit of order exactly pᵏ⁻¹(p − 1)), and concrete evaluations.
overview.proofStrategy: The engine is Mathlib's ZMod.isCyclic_units_of_prime_pow (the odd prime-power unit group is cyclic) combined with IsCyclic.iff_exponent_eq_card (a finite cyclic group's exponent equals its cardinality). Since λ = ArithmeticFunction.Carmichael is by definition that exponent (carmichael_eq_exponent') and φ(pᵏ) = #(ℤ/pᵏℤ)ˣ (ZMod.card_units_eq_totient), this gives λ(pᵏ) = φ(pᵏ); the totient prime-power formula Nat.totient_prime_pow then yields pᵏ⁻¹(p − 1). The primitive root comes from IsCyclic.exists_ofOrder_eq_natCard, transporting the generator's order through the same card = totient identity. Concrete values instantiate the formula and reduce powers by norm_num.
keyInsights: The single fact doing the work is exponent = order, which holds precisely because (ℤ/pᵏℤ)ˣ is cyclic; everything else is bookkeeping (λ = exponent, φ = order).
Odd prime powers are the cyclic regime, opposite to the 2-power case of the parent: there λ = φ/2 because the group splits as ℤ/2 × ℤ/2ᵏ⁻², here λ = φ because the group is a single cycle.
Making λ(pᵏ) an explicit polynomial pᵏ⁻¹(p − 1) — rather than the implicit value φ(pᵏ) — is what the parent left undone; it is the honest answer to 'what is λ on an odd prime power'.
Cyclicity is constructive enough to name a witness: a primitive root mod pᵏ is an actual unit of order exactly φ(pᵏ), recovered from the cyclic generator.
λ(p) = p − 1 is the k = 1 corollary: (ℤ/pℤ)ˣ is the multiplicative group of a finite field, cyclic of order p − 1.
prerequisites: The unit group (ℤ/nℤ)ˣ, its order φ(n), and the Carmichael function λ as its exponent
Cyclic groups: a finite cyclic group's exponent equals its order, and it has a generator of that order
Gauss's theorem that (ℤ/pᵏℤ)ˣ is cyclic for an odd prime p (primitive roots exist)
The totient prime-power formula φ(pᵏ) = pᵏ⁻¹(p − 1)

conclusion.summary: A fully verified (0 sorries, 0 axioms, no native_decide) file of 122 lines and 11 theorems giving the Carmichael function on odd prime powers in closed form: λ(pᵏ) = pᵏ⁻¹(p − 1) for an odd prime p and k ≥ 1, with the cyclic mechanism (exponent = order), the k = 1 case λ(p) = p − 1, the existence of a primitive root of order exactly φ(pᵏ), and the concrete values λ(9)=6, λ(27)=18, λ(25)=20, λ(7)=6, λ(49)=42.
conclusion.implications: This completes the odd half of the parent's prime-power Carmichael analysis: where the parent stopped at the implicit λ(pᵏ) = φ(pᵏ), λ is now an explicit polynomial, and the structural cause (cyclicity ⟹ exponent = order) is exhibited rather than asserted. Together with the parent's λ(2ᵏ) = 2ᵏ⁻² and Mathlib's lcm formula carmichael_factorization, λ is now determined in closed form at every prime power, hence (by lcm) at every n. The primitive-root existence result partially answers the parent's own follow-up question on characterizing n with primitive roots.
openQuestions: Assemble the full closed form for λ(n) at arbitrary n by feeding the prime-power values pᵏ⁻¹(p − 1) (odd p) and 2ᵏ⁻² (p = 2, k ≥ 3) into carmichael_factorization's lcm.
Characterize exactly the moduli n admitting a primitive root (n ∈ {1, 2, 4, pᵏ, 2pᵏ} for odd primes p), using the cyclic/non-cyclic dichotomy between odd prime powers and powers of two.
